questions.stem: Which command creates a SYMBOLIC link named /usr/local/bin/python that points to /usr/bin/python3.11, so the target can live on a different filesystem?

explanation.correct: ln -s TARGET LINKNAME creates a symbolic (soft) link. Because it stores a path, not an inode, it may cross filesystems and point at directories.

distractors.A: ln without -s makes a HARD link, which shares the inode and cannot span filesystems or link directories.
distractors.B: cp -s does exist in GNU cp but is non-portable and unusual; ln -s is the standard, expected tool.
distractors.C: link (and the link() call) creates a HARD link only; it cannot make a symlink.

explanation.exam_pattern: Symlink = ln -s (path-based, cross-filesystem); hard link = ln (shared inode, same filesystem).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Manage files and directories (ln -s)

questions.stem: Which command displays a file's inode number, size, permissions, and its access, modify, and change timestamps in one detailed report? (command name only)

explanation.correct: stat FILE prints the inode, size, block count, permission bits (octal and symbolic), owner/group, and the atime/mtime/ctime timestamps.
explanation.exam_pattern: stat = full metadata/inode/timestamps for one file; ls -l = compact listing.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — File metadata (stat)

questions.stem: Which command creates a single gzip-compressed archive named backup.tar.gz from the directory /etc?

explanation.correct: tar -c creates an archive, -z pipes it through gzip, and -f names the output file, so -czf backup.tar.gz /etc builds the compressed tarball.

distractors.A: -x EXTRACTS from an existing archive rather than creating one.
distractors.B: -t only LISTS the table of contents of an archive; it creates nothing.
distractors.C: gzip compresses individual files in place and does not bundle a directory tree into one tar archive.

explanation.exam_pattern: tar: -c create, -x extract, -t list; add -z (gzip) or -j (bzip2); -f names the file.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Archiving/compression (tar)

questions.stem: Per the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, which top-level directory is reserved for optional, self-contained add-on application software packages (for example a vendor that installs everything under one subdirectory)?

explanation.correct: /opt holds optional/add-on software, typically each package in its own /opt/<vendor> subtree, keeping third-party software separate from the distribution's files.

distractors.A: /srv holds data served by the system (e.g., web or FTP content), not installed application binaries.
distractors.B: /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information, not software.
distractors.C: /mnt is a temporary mount point for manually mounted filesystems.

explanation.exam_pattern: /opt = add-on packages; /srv = served data; /usr/local = locally compiled software; /mnt = temp mounts.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (/opt)

questions.stem: Which command recursively searches every file under /etc for lines containing the text 'nameserver' and prints each match with its filename and line number?

explanation.correct: grep -r recurses into the directory tree and -n prefixes each match with its line number; the filename is shown automatically when more than one file is searched.

distractors.A: Plain grep on a directory errors (or is skipped) without -r/-R; it does not recurse by default.
distractors.B: locate searches a prebuilt filename database for paths; it does not grep file contents.
distractors.C: find -name matches file NAMES, not text inside files.

explanation.exam_pattern: Search file CONTENTS recursively with grep -r (add -n lines, -i ignore case, -l names only).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Searching text (grep -r)

questions.stem: You must mirror /data to /backup/data so the copy preserves permissions, ownership, symlinks, and timestamps and only transfers changed files on repeat runs. Which command is best?

explanation.correct: rsync -a (archive mode) is recursive and preserves permissions, ownership, symlinks, and times; on later runs it copies only the differences, making it ideal for mirroring.

distractors.A: mv MOVES the data (removing the source); it does not keep a maintained copy.
distractors.C: Plain cp (without -a/-r) will not even recurse into the directory and preserves nothing special.
distractors.D: scp copies over SSH but is not delta-based and does not efficiently re-sync only changes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Efficient mirror preserving attributes = rsync -a; add --delete to remove extras, -z to compress.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — File synchronization (rsync)

questions.stem: On a RHEL 9 host you have the path /usr/sbin/semanage but do not know which package supplies it. Which command identifies the package that PROVIDES that file, even if it is not yet installed?

explanation.correct: dnf provides <path> (alias 'dnf whatprovides') searches repository metadata for the package that supplies a file or capability, whether or not it is installed.

distractors.A: dnf search matches names and summaries by keyword, not a specific file path.
distractors.B: rpm -qf only works if the file is ALREADY installed on disk; it queries the local RPM DB, not repos.
distractors.D: dnf list installed reports installed packages by name; it does not map a file path to a package.

explanation.exam_pattern: File path -> package: 'dnf provides <path>' (from repos) or 'rpm -qf <path>' (if installed).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Software management (dnf provides)

questions.stem: An installed binary at /usr/bin/ss is misbehaving and you want to know which RPM owns it on a RHEL system. Which command answers that?

explanation.correct: rpm -qf <file> queries which installed package OWNS the given file path (here it reports the iproute package).

distractors.A: rpm -ql lists the FILES in a named package; it expects a package name, not a path, and does the reverse lookup.
distractors.C: rpm -V VERIFIES a package's files against the DB (size/mode/checksum); it does not report the owner.
distractors.D: rpm -qi shows package INFO (description, version) for a named package, not file ownership.

explanation.exam_pattern: rpm query flags: -qf file->package, -ql package->files, -qi info, -qa all, -V verify.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Software management (rpm -qf)

questions.stem: On Debian/Ubuntu, which command refreshes the local package index from the configured repositories WITHOUT upgrading any installed packages?

explanation.correct: apt update re-downloads the package lists so apt knows the latest available versions; it changes no installed software. You then run 'apt upgrade' to apply updates.

distractors.B: apt upgrade installs newer versions of already-installed packages; it does not refresh the index itself.
distractors.C: apt install --reinstall reinstalls a named package; it is unrelated to refreshing the index.
distractors.D: apt full-upgrade upgrades and may add/remove packages to resolve changes; it also installs, not just indexes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Debian flow: 'apt update' (refresh lists) THEN 'apt upgrade' (apply). Fedora's 'dnf upgrade' does both.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Software management (apt update vs upgrade)

questions.stem: On Debian/Ubuntu, which command searches the APT package cache for available packages whose name or description mentions 'nginx'? (command and subcommand, two words)

explanation.correct: apt search <term> (or the older 'apt-cache search <term>') lists available packages whose name or description matches the term, helping you find the right package to install.
explanation.exam_pattern: Find a package: 'apt search' (Debian) / 'dnf search' (Fedora); install with apt/dnf install.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Software management (apt search)

questions.stem: A dnf upgrade on a RHEL host broke an application, and you need to roll back the most recent transaction. Which command set does this?

options.text: dnf history, then dnf history undo <id>

explanation.correct: dnf history lists past transactions with their IDs, and 'dnf history undo <id>' reverses that specific transaction (reinstalling/removing packages to the prior state).

distractors.A: dnf downgrade lowers a package to an earlier version but has no '--rollback' option tied to a transaction.
distractors.B: rpm -e erases packages and has no transaction-based '--rollback' (that depended on an unused rpm feature).
distractors.D: dnf remove --all-versions is not a rollback; it would uninstall packages, not restore prior versions.

explanation.exam_pattern: dnf/yum keep a transaction log: 'dnf history' to view, 'dnf history undo <id>' to reverse one.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Software management (dnf history)

questions.stem: Which command installs the sandboxed desktop application org.gimp.GIMP from the Flathub remote using the distribution-agnostic Flatpak system?

explanation.correct: flatpak install <remote> <app-id> pulls the application (and its runtime) from the named remote; Flathub is the common community remote.

distractors.B: flatpak run LAUNCHES an already-installed app; it does not install it, and takes an app-id, not a remote.
distractors.C: snap is a different (Canonical) packaging system and uses snap names, not Flatpak app-IDs/remotes.
distractors.D: dnf has no 'flatpak' subcommand; Flatpak is managed by the flatpak tool, not dnf.

explanation.exam_pattern: Flatpak: 'flatpak install <remote> <app-id>' then 'flatpak run <app-id>'; Snap uses 'snap install'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Universal packages (Flatpak)

questions.stem: Issuing 'kill 2200' with no signal option sends which signal, allowing the process to clean up before exiting?

explanation.correct: The default signal for kill is SIGTERM (15): a polite request to terminate that a process can trap to flush buffers and shut down cleanly.

distractors.A: SIGHUP (1) traditionally means hangup and is often used to make daemons reload config, not the default.
distractors.B: SIGKILL (9) is the FORCEFUL kill that cannot be caught or ignored; it is sent only with 'kill -9'.
distractors.D: SIGSTOP (19) only PAUSES a process (resumable with SIGCONT); it does not terminate it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default kill = SIGTERM (15, graceful). Use SIGKILL (9) only when SIGTERM is ignored.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Signals (kill/SIGTERM)

questions.stem: Several java processes are stuck and you want to terminate every process whose full command line contains 'oldapp.jar', without looking up PIDs. Which command does this?

explanation.correct: pkill -f matches the pattern against the FULL command line and signals all matches (default SIGTERM), so processes launched as 'java ... oldapp.jar' are caught.

distractors.A: kill takes a numeric PID, not a name/pattern, so 'kill oldapp.jar' fails.
distractors.B: killall matches the process NAME (e.g., 'java'), not arguments, so 'oldapp.jar' as a name won't match.
distractors.D: pgrep -f only LISTS the matching PIDs; it sends no signal (pgrep finds, pkill kills).

explanation.exam_pattern: pgrep/pkill find/kill by name or, with -f, by full command line; killall matches the exact process name.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Process control (pkill -f)

questions.stem: On a systemd host, which command lists the active timer units along with when each last ran and when it is next scheduled to run (the systemd alternative to cron)?

explanation.correct: systemctl list-timers shows each active .timer unit with NEXT and LAST run times and the service it activates; timers are systemd's scheduling mechanism.

distractors.A: crontab -l lists the invoking user's cron jobs, a separate scheduler, not systemd timers.
distractors.B: list-units --type=service shows services, not timer units or their schedule.
distractors.D: systemd-analyze reports boot performance; it does not list timers and their next runs.

explanation.exam_pattern: systemd scheduling: a .timer unit activates a matching .service; inspect with 'systemctl list-timers'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Scheduling (systemd timers)

questions.stem: You start a long backup over SSH and need it to keep running after you log out, with its output saved to a file. Which invocation is correct?

explanation.correct: nohup makes the command ignore the SIGHUP sent at logout, '&' runs it in the background, and output is redirected to nohup.out by default, so it survives the session.

distractors.A: '&& exit' just closes the shell after the script finishes in the FOREGROUND; it never detaches it.
distractors.B: '&' alone backgrounds the job, but it can still receive SIGHUP and die when the shell exits (unless huponexit is off).
distractors.C: bg resumes an ALREADY-stopped job in the background; it does not launch a new command or protect from HUP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Survive logout: 'nohup cmd &' or 'systemd-run'/disown; terminal multiplexers (tmux/screen) also work.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Background jobs (nohup)

questions.stem: After editing /etc/nginx/nginx.conf you want nginx to re-read its configuration WITHOUT dropping existing client connections. Which systemd action is appropriate?

explanation.correct: systemctl reload triggers the unit's ExecReload (for nginx, a graceful config reload) so the service applies new settings without a full restart or dropped connections.

distractors.A: daemon-reload reloads systemd's own UNIT files after you change a .service file; it does not reload nginx.conf.
distractors.C: stop shuts the service down entirely rather than reloading it.
distractors.D: restart fully stops and starts the service, briefly interrupting active connections.

explanation.exam_pattern: reload = re-read app config in place; restart = stop+start; daemon-reload = re-read systemd unit files.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Manage services (systemctl reload)

questions.stem: Which command displays running processes as a tree, showing the parent/child relationships (which process spawned which)? (command name only)

explanation.correct: pstree draws the process hierarchy, visually linking each child to the parent that forked it; 'pstree -p' adds PIDs.
explanation.exam_pattern: pstree = parent/child tree view; 'ps --forest' (or ps axjf) shows a similar hierarchy.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Process hierarchy (pstree)

questions.stem: Security policy requires that user 'svc' must change its password at least every 60 days. Which command sets that maximum password age?

explanation.correct: chage -M 60 sets the MAXIMUM number of days a password is valid before a change is forced; 'chage -l svc' shows the resulting aging fields.

distractors.A: chage -m (lowercase) sets the MINIMUM days between changes, not the maximum lifetime.
distractors.B: chage -d sets the date of the LAST password change (used to force an immediate change), not the maximum age.
distractors.D: usermod -e sets an account EXPIRATION DATE (a calendar date), not the password change interval.

explanation.exam_pattern: chage: -M max age, -m min age, -W warn days, -E account expiry date, -l list.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Password aging (chage -M)

questions.stem: A departing employee's account 'jsmith' must be removed together with its home directory and mail spool. Which single command does this?

explanation.correct: userdel -r removes the account AND deletes its home directory and mail spool, leaving no leftover files behind.

distractors.A: userdel without -r deletes the account entry but LEAVES the home directory and its files in place.
distractors.B: rm -rf deletes the home files but leaves the account defined in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.
distractors.D: usermod -L only LOCKS the password; the account and files remain.

explanation.exam_pattern: userdel -r = account + home + mail spool; plain userdel keeps the home directory.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Manage users (userdel -r)

questions.stem: Which directory holds the skeleton files (such as .bashrc and .profile) that useradd copies into a new user's home directory when it is created? (full path)

explanation.correct: /etc/skel is the template: its contents are copied into each new home directory created with 'useradd -m', giving new users a consistent starting environment.
explanation.exam_pattern: New-home template = /etc/skel; account defaults = /etc/default/useradd and /etc/login.defs.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — User defaults (/etc/skel)

questions.stem: On a host joined to LDAP/SSSD, 'grep alice /etc/passwd' returns nothing, yet alice can log in. Which command correctly looks up her account through ALL configured name sources (local files plus directory services)?

explanation.correct: getent queries the NSS stack defined in /etc/nsswitch.conf, so 'getent passwd alice' returns her entry whether it comes from local files, LDAP, or SSSD.

distractors.B: Reading /etc/passwd only sees LOCAL accounts, missing directory-provided users like alice.
distractors.C: lsof -u lists a user's open files; it does not resolve account database entries.
distractors.D: id -u expects a username and returns a UID; passing a file path is meaningless here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Resolve accounts across files + LDAP/SSSD with getent (passwd/group/hosts); it honors nsswitch.conf.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Name service lookups (getent)

questions.stem: What is the key difference when you switch to another user with 'su - bob' compared with 'su bob'?

options.text: 'su - bob' starts a LOGIN shell: it loads bob's environment and changes to bob's home directory
There is no functional difference; the dash is cosmetic
'su - bob' keeps your current environment and directory; 'su bob' resets them
'su - bob' requires bob's password, while 'su bob' uses your own

explanation.correct: The dash makes su start a LOGIN shell, so it reads bob's login profile, sets his PATH/HOME, and moves to his home directory — as if bob had logged in directly.

distractors.B: The dash is significant: it controls whether a login environment is loaded.
distractors.C: This is reversed: 'su bob' (no dash) keeps your environment; 'su - bob' resets it to bob's login environment.
distractors.D: Both forms prompt for the TARGET user's password (bob's); the dash does not change which password is required.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'su -' (or 'su -l') = full login environment + target's home; 'su' keeps your current env/cwd.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Switching users (su -)

questions.stem: After 'lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/data' succeeds, the mounted filesystem still shows the old size. Which TWO commands can grow the filesystem onto the new space, depending on its type? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: An ext filesystem is grown with resize2fs on the device, while XFS is grown with xfs_growfs given its MOUNT POINT; both can expand online to fill the enlarged LV.

distractors.A: mkfs.ext4 would CREATE a new filesystem on the LV, destroying all existing data.
distractors.D: fdisk edits partition tables on whole disks; it does not resize a filesystem on a logical volume.

explanation.exam_pattern: After lvextend, grow the fs: resize2fs (ext) or xfs_growfs (XFS); 'lvextend -r' can do both in one step.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Grow filesystems (resize2fs/xfs_growfs)

questions.stem: Which command prints block devices with their UUID, filesystem TYPE, and LABEL — the values you copy into /etc/fstab for persistent mounts? (command name only)

explanation.correct: blkid reports each block device's UUID, TYPE, and LABEL, so you can reference a filesystem by UUID= in /etc/fstab instead of an unstable /dev name.
explanation.exam_pattern: Get a UUID for fstab with blkid (or 'lsblk -f'); prefer UUID=/LABEL= over /dev/sdXN.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Identify filesystems (blkid)

questions.stem: You added a new partition /dev/sdb2 to use as additional swap. Which sequence formats it as swap and activates it immediately?

explanation.correct: mkswap writes a swap signature to the device, then swapon enables it for paging; add an entry to /etc/fstab (with 'swap' as the type) to make it persist across reboots.

distractors.A: There is no mkfs.swap, and swap areas are activated with swapon, not mount.
distractors.B: The order is wrong: you must mkswap (format) BEFORE swapon (activate).
distractors.D: fallocate pre-allocates a file's size and is used for swap FILES, not to format a partition; swapon -a only re-reads fstab.

explanation.exam_pattern: Swap partition: mkswap then swapon (add to fstab to persist); 'swapon --show' / 'free -h' to verify.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Swap space (mkswap/swapon)

questions.stem: Before a risky upgrade you want a point-in-time LVM snapshot named data_snap of the logical volume /dev/vg0/data so you can roll back. Which command creates it?

explanation.correct: lvcreate -s (snapshot) -n names it, -L sizes the copy-on-write area, and the origin LV is the final argument, producing /dev/vg0/data_snap for rollback or backup.

distractors.A: lvconvert changes volume types (e.g., mirror/thin) and is not the standard way to create a snapshot.
distractors.C: vgcreate creates a VOLUME GROUP; -s there sets the physical extent size, unrelated to snapshots.
distractors.D: Without -s this creates a brand-new ordinary logical volume, not a snapshot of the origin.

explanation.exam_pattern: LVM snapshot = 'lvcreate -s -n <name> -L <size> <origin-LV>'; merge back with lvconvert --merge.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — LVM snapshots (lvcreate -s)

questions.stem: A volume group vg0 is out of free extents. You have initialized a new physical volume /dev/sdd1 with pvcreate. Which command adds that PV's capacity to vg0?

explanation.correct: vgextend adds one or more physical volumes to an existing volume group, increasing the free extents available for logical volumes.

distractors.A: There is no pvextend command; pvresize exists but only re-reads a PV's own size.
distractors.B: vgmerge combines two existing VOLUME GROUPS, not a VG and a bare PV.
distractors.D: lvextend grows a LOGICAL VOLUME; it cannot add a PV to the group.

explanation.exam_pattern: Grow a VG: pvcreate the disk, then 'vgextend <vg> <pv>'; then lvextend the LV into the new space.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Extend volume groups (vgextend)

questions.stem: You just added a new line to /etc/fstab for an extra data disk. Which command mounts ALL currently-unmounted fstab entries, letting you confirm the new entry works without rebooting?

explanation.correct: mount -a reads /etc/fstab and mounts every entry not already mounted (and not marked noauto), so a typo in the new line surfaces immediately instead of at the next boot.

distractors.A: mount --bind re-mounts an existing directory elsewhere; it does not process fstab entries.
distractors.B: remount / only re-applies options to the already-mounted root; it does not process the new entry.
distractors.D: daemon-reload re-reads systemd units; although systemd generates mount units from fstab, 'mount -a' is the direct test.

explanation.exam_pattern: Test a new fstab line safely with 'mount -a' (and 'findmnt --verify') before relying on it at boot.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Mounting filesystems (mount -a)

questions.stem: Which command persistently sets the system's static hostname to web01 on a modern systemd distribution, updating /etc/hostname?

explanation.correct: hostnamectl set-hostname web01 updates the static hostname in /etc/hostname (and the live kernel value), so it persists across reboots.

distractors.B: The legacy 'hostname web01' changes the name only until the next reboot; it is not persistent.
distractors.C: sysctl kernel.hostname sets the RUNNING kernel value only; it does not write /etc/hostname, so it is lost on reboot.
distractors.D: Writing to /proc sets the running name temporarily and does not update the config file.

explanation.exam_pattern: Persistent hostname = hostnamectl set-hostname (writes /etc/hostname); plain 'hostname' is temporary.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Hostname (hostnamectl)

questions.stem: You need a host to resolve the name 'build.internal' to 10.0.5.20 locally, taking precedence over DNS and without running a DNS server. Which file do you edit?

explanation.correct: /etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses locally. With the default nsswitch order (files before dns), an entry here is used before any DNS query.

distractors.A: /etc/resolv.conf lists the DNS NAMESERVERS to query; it does not hold static name-to-IP entries.
distractors.B: /etc/hostname stores THIS machine's own hostname, not mappings for other hosts.
distractors.D: /etc/networks maps names to NETWORK numbers, not individual host addresses.

explanation.exam_pattern: Static local name->IP = /etc/hosts (checked before DNS); DNS servers = /etc/resolv.conf.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Local name resolution (/etc/hosts)

questions.stem: A host has an IP but no default gateway. Using iproute2, which command adds a default route via the gateway 192.168.10.1 on interface eth0 for the current session?

options.text: ip addr add default 192.168.10.1 dev eth0
ip route add default via 192.168.10.1 dev eth0

explanation.correct: ip route add default via <gateway> dev <iface> installs the default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing at the next-hop gateway, enabling traffic to other networks.

distractors.A: The keyword order is wrong; the destination 'default' comes first, then 'via <gw> dev <iface>'.
distractors.B: ip addr manages interface ADDRESSES, not routes; 'default' is not valid syntax there.
distractors.C: 'route default ...' is not valid; the legacy form was 'route add default gw <ip>', and route is deprecated.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default gateway (runtime): 'ip route add default via <gw> dev <iface>'; persist via NetworkManager/netplan.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Routing (ip route add default)

questions.stem: On a NetworkManager-managed system, which command lists the network devices and shows each one's type, state (connected/disconnected), and the connection in use?

explanation.correct: nmcli device status lists each interface with its DEVICE, TYPE, STATE, and the active CONNECTION profile, the quick way to see what NetworkManager thinks is up.

distractors.B: nmcli radio all reports the on/off state of WiFi/WWAN radios, not per-device status.
distractors.C: nmcli connection reload re-reads profile files from disk; it displays nothing about device state.
distractors.D: ip -s link shows interface statistics (packets/errors), not NetworkManager connection state.

explanation.exam_pattern: nmcli device status (devices/state) vs nmcli connection show (profiles); 'nmcli con up <name>' activates.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — NetworkManager (nmcli device status)

questions.stem: An interface eth1 shows state DOWN in 'ip link'. Using iproute2, which command administratively brings the link up?

explanation.correct: ip link set <iface> up changes the interface's administrative state to UP; 'ip link set eth1 down' takes it back down.

distractors.A: ifup is the older ifupdown/distro tool and may be absent; the iproute2 way is 'ip link set ... up'.
distractors.B: 'ip link eth1 enable' is invalid syntax; the verb is 'set <dev> up'.
distractors.D: ip addr manages addresses; 'up' is not an ip addr operation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Toggle a link with 'ip link set <iface> up|down'; confirm with 'ip link show'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Interface state (ip link set)

questions.stem: Which command prints just the version (release) string of the currently running kernel, for example 5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64? (command and flag)

explanation.correct: uname -r outputs the running kernel release string. ('uname -a' prints everything; 'uname -m' the machine architecture.)
explanation.exam_pattern: Running kernel version = 'uname -r'; installed kernels (RHEL) via 'rpm -q kernel'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Kernel version (uname -r)

questions.stem: A server should boot to a full graphical desktop by default (the equivalent of the old runlevel 5). Which command sets that systemd default target?

explanation.correct: systemctl set-default graphical.target makes the graphical target (≈ runlevel 5) the default at boot by relinking /etc/systemd/system/default.target.

distractors.A: multi-user.target is the non-graphical, text/networked target (≈ runlevel 3) — the opposite request.
distractors.C: enable arranges a unit to start via its install dependencies; it does not set the default boot target.
distractors.D: isolate switches to the target NOW for the current session but does not change the boot DEFAULT.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default boot target: 'systemctl set-default graphical.target' (RL5) or multi-user.target (RL3); isolate = now only.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — systemd targets (set-default)

questions.stem: A faulty driver module 'nouveau' must be UNLOADED from the running kernel right now (you will blacklist it separately). Which command removes the loaded module?

explanation.correct: modprobe -r unloads the module and any now-unused dependencies (equivalent to rmmod but dependency-aware). To keep it from loading at boot, add it to /etc/modprobe.d/ with 'blacklist nouveau'.

distractors.A: modprobe nouveau (no -r) LOADS the module, the opposite of unloading it.
distractors.B: depmod rebuilds the modules.dep dependency map; it does not load or unload modules.
distractors.D: insmod has no -r unload option; it only inserts a single .ko and ignores dependencies.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unload now: 'modprobe -r <mod>' (or rmmod). Prevent at boot: 'blacklist <mod>' in /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Kernel modules (modprobe -r)

questions.stem: After adding a storage driver to the module load list, a RHEL/Fedora system must rebuild its initramfs so the driver is available early in boot. Which command does this?

explanation.correct: On RHEL/Fedora, dracut builds the initramfs; 'dracut -f' forces an overwrite of the existing image for the current kernel so the new module is included at early boot.

distractors.A: grub2-mkconfig regenerates the bootloader menu, not the initramfs image.
distractors.B: mkfs creates a filesystem; it has nothing to do with generating an initramfs.
distractors.D: update-initramfs is the DEBIAN/Ubuntu tool; it is normally absent on RHEL/Fedora.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rebuild initramfs: dracut -f (RHEL/Fedora) vs update-initramfs -u (Debian/Ubuntu).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — initramfs (dracut)

questions.stem: A server crashed and rebooted. Which journalctl command shows the logs from the PREVIOUS boot (the one that ended in the crash), assuming persistent journaling is enabled?

explanation.correct: journalctl -b -1 selects the previous boot (-b 0 or -b is the current boot). 'journalctl --list-boots' enumerates the boots and their offsets.

distractors.A: -k limits output to kernel messages for the current boot; it does not select a previous boot.
distractors.C: --rotate rotates the journal FILES; it displays no logs.
distractors.D: journalctl -b (or -b 0) shows the CURRENT boot, not the crashed prior one.

explanation.exam_pattern: Previous boot logs: 'journalctl -b -1' (needs persistent journal: Storage=persistent / /var/log/journal).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 1 — Boot logs (journalctl -b -1)

questions.stem: A user's umask is 022. When that user creates a NEW regular file (before any later chmod), what permissions does it receive?

explanation.correct: New files start from base 666; the umask masks off the bits, so 666 minus 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--). (New directories start from 777, giving 755 under the same umask.)

distractors.A: 664 would come from umask 002, not 022.
distractors.B: 755 is the result for a new DIRECTORY (777 - 022), not a regular file, which never gets execute by default.
distractors.D: 600 would require a umask of 077, which masks all group/other bits.

explanation.exam_pattern: File perms = 666 - umask; directory perms = 777 - umask. umask 022 -> 644 files / 755 dirs.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Default permissions (umask)

questions.stem: A shared project directory /srv/team must ensure every NEW file and subdirectory created inside it automatically belongs to the directory's group. Which command sets the bit that does this?

explanation.correct: The SGID bit on a directory (chmod g+s, or the 2 in 2775) makes new entries inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group — ideal for shared workspaces.

distractors.A: SUID (u+s) on a directory has no group-inheritance effect; on files it runs them as the owner.
distractors.B: The sticky bit (+t) restricts deletion to file owners; it does not control group inheritance.
distractors.C: g+w merely grants group WRITE; it does not make new files inherit the directory's group.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shared-group directory = SGID (chmod g+s / 2xxx); files then inherit the dir's group.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Special permissions (SGID directory)

questions.stem: During a security audit you must list every regular file on the system that has the SUID bit set (a common privilege-escalation review). Which command does this?

explanation.correct: -perm -4000 matches files that have (at least) the SUID bit set; the leading minus means 'all of these bits present', so it finds set-user-ID binaries anywhere on /.

distractors.A: -perm 777 matches files whose permissions are EXACTLY rwxrwxrwx, missing SUID files and catching unrelated ones.
distractors.B: Grepping ls output for 'rwx' is unreliable and does not isolate the SUID 's' bit.
distractors.D: -perm -2000 finds SGID (set-group-ID) files, not SUID.

explanation.exam_pattern: Audit SUID/SGID: 'find / -perm -4000' (SUID) and 'find / -perm -2000' (SGID); -perm -1000 = sticky.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Special permissions (find -perm -4000)

questions.stem: Which single command changes BOTH the owner to 'bob' and the group to 'staff' on the file project.txt?

explanation.correct: chown accepts owner:group in one argument, so 'chown bob:staff project.txt' sets the owner to bob and the group to staff simultaneously.

distractors.A: chgrp changes only the GROUP and does not take an owner:group pair.
distractors.B: Without the colon, 'bob' and 'staff' are read as two separate path/user arguments and it fails.
distractors.C: chmod changes permission BITS, not ownership.

explanation.exam_pattern: chown owner:group sets both; chown owner sets owner only; chgrp or 'chown :group' sets group only.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Ownership (chown owner:group)

questions.stem: On the directory /shared you want the group 'devs' to automatically receive rwx on every file created there in the future, via a DEFAULT ACL. Which command sets it?

explanation.correct: The -d flag sets a DEFAULT ACL on the directory, which is inherited by newly created entries, so future files grant devs rwx automatically.

distractors.A: -b REMOVES all ACL entries rather than adding a default one.
distractors.B: chmod cannot create an inheritable default for a specific named group; it changes current bits only.
distractors.D: Without -d this sets an ACL on the directory itself only; existing/new files inside do not inherit it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inheritable ACL = 'setfacl -d -m ...' (default ACL on a directory); -m current, -x remove, -b clear.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Default ACLs (setfacl -d)

questions.stem: The command 'ls -l /usr/bin/passwd' shows -rwsr-xr-x. Why must /usr/bin/passwd have the SUID bit (the 's' in the owner's execute position)?

options.text: So the file cannot be deleted by non-owners
So only root can execute the file
So the file inherits the group of its parent directory
So any user running it executes with the file owner's (root's) privileges, letting them update /etc/shadow

explanation.correct: SUID makes the program run with the privileges of its OWNER (root for passwd), so an ordinary user can change their hashed password in the root-only /etc/shadow.

distractors.A: Delete protection in a shared directory is the sticky bit, not SUID.
distractors.B: r-x for group/other means others CAN execute it; SUID is about the privilege it runs with, not who may run it.
distractors.C: That describes SGID on a directory, not SUID on an executable.

explanation.exam_pattern: SUID (chmod u+s / 4xxx) = run as the file's owner; classic example is /usr/bin/passwd owned by root.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Special permissions (SUID)

questions.stem: In /etc/sudoers, which line grants EVERY member of the 'wheel' group the ability to run any command as any user via sudo?

explanation.correct: The leading % marks a GROUP. '%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL' lets wheel members run all commands, as any target user, on all hosts.

distractors.B: @ is not the group prefix (it is %), and NOPASSWD must precede a command list, so this line is malformed.
distractors.C: Without the %, 'wheel' is treated as a USER name, not the group, so it does not grant the group.
distractors.D: This is not valid sudoers syntax; a rule needs the host=(runas) command fields.

explanation.exam_pattern: sudoers: %group for a group; user host=(runas) commands; 'NOPASSWD:' before commands skips the password.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Privilege delegation (sudoers %group)

questions.stem: Apache (httpd) needs to make outbound network connections, but SELinux is blocking it. Which command enables the relevant SELinux boolean PERSISTENTLY across reboots?

explanation.correct: setsebool -P writes the boolean to persistent policy so it survives reboots; here it lets httpd open network connections.

distractors.B: getsebool READS a boolean's current value; it does not change it.
distractors.C: The syntax is incomplete/incorrect; booleans are toggled with setsebool (-P to persist), not 'semanage boolean <name>' alone.
distractors.D: Without -P the change is runtime-only and is lost at the next reboot.

explanation.exam_pattern: SELinux booleans: 'getsebool -a' to view, 'setsebool -P <bool> on' to set persistently.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SELinux booleans (setsebool -P)

questions.stem: Which command shows the SELinux security context (user:role:type:level) of the files in the current directory?

explanation.correct: ls -Z appends each file's SELinux context; the type field (e.g., httpd_sys_content_t) is what SELinux checks. 'ps -Z' and 'id -Z' show process and user contexts.

distractors.A: stat -c %a prints the octal permission bits, not the SELinux label.
distractors.C: ls -l shows the standard DAC permissions, owner, and group but not the SELinux context.
distractors.D: ls -i shows inode numbers, not security contexts.

explanation.exam_pattern: View SELinux labels with -Z: 'ls -Z' (files), 'ps -Z' (processes), 'id -Z' (your context).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SELinux contexts (ls -Z)

questions.stem: You configured a web app to listen on TCP 8090, but with SELinux enforcing, httpd cannot bind to it. Which command adds 8090 to the allowed http port type so the service can bind?

explanation.correct: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8090 labels TCP 8090 as an http port type, so SELinux permits httpd to bind it. (If the port already has a type, use -m to modify.)

distractors.A: setsebool toggles boolean switches; it does not map a port number to a type.
distractors.B: firewall-cmd opens the port in the FIREWALL; it does not change the SELinux port label that is blocking the bind.
distractors.D: restorecon relabels FILES to their default context; it does not manage port labels.

explanation.exam_pattern: Nonstandard service port under SELinux: 'semanage port -a -t <type> -p tcp <port>' (then open the firewall).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SELinux port labeling (semanage port)

questions.stem: On an Ubuntu host you want the AppArmor profile for nginx to actively BLOCK (not just log) policy violations. Which command puts that profile into enforce mode?

explanation.correct: aa-enforce switches the named AppArmor profile to enforce mode, where violations are denied and logged. aa-complain would only log them.

distractors.A: aa-complain puts the profile in COMPLAIN mode: it permits and merely logs violations — the opposite of blocking.
distractors.C: setenforce is an SELinux command; it has no effect on AppArmor profiles.
distractors.D: aa-disable UNLOADS the profile entirely, removing protection rather than enforcing it.

explanation.exam_pattern: AppArmor modes: aa-enforce (block), aa-complain (log only), aa-disable (unload); check with aa-status.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — AppArmor enforcement (aa-enforce)

questions.stem: You added several firewalld rules in the RUNTIME configuration only (no --permanent) and they work. Which command saves the current runtime rules into the permanent configuration so they survive a reboot?

explanation.correct: firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent copies the active runtime ruleset into the permanent config, preserving changes you made without --permanent.

distractors.A: --reload REPLACES the runtime config with the permanent one, DISCARDING your unsaved runtime rules.
distractors.B: --permanent --reload is not a valid combination for saving; --reload always applies permanent over runtime.
distractors.C: Restarting firewalld reloads permanent rules and loses the runtime-only changes, just like --reload.

explanation.exam_pattern: Save runtime rules: '--runtime-to-permanent'. '--reload' goes the other way (permanent -> runtime).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — firewalld persistence (runtime-to-permanent)

questions.stem: A custom service listens on TCP 8080. Which firewalld command permanently opens that specific port (not a predefined service name) in the default zone?

explanation.correct: --add-port takes port/protocol, so '--permanent --add-port=8080/tcp' opens TCP 8080; follow with 'firewall-cmd --reload' to activate it.

distractors.B: --add-service expects a named service (like http), not a bare port number.
distractors.C: '/all' is not a valid protocol; it must be tcp, udp, sctp, or dccp.
distractors.D: A port rule requires the protocol (8080/tcp or 8080/udp); '8080' alone is invalid, and without --permanent it is runtime-only.

explanation.exam_pattern: Open a raw port: '--add-port=<port>/<proto>'; open a known service: '--add-service=<name>'; then --reload.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — firewalld ports (--add-port)

questions.stem: Which firewalld command changes the DEFAULT zone (the zone applied to interfaces not explicitly assigned) to 'dmz'?

explanation.correct: firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=dmz sets the default zone immediately and permanently (it is one of the few settings applied to both at once).

distractors.B: --new-zone CREATES a new (empty) zone definition; it does not make it the default.
distractors.C: --change-interface reassigns a specific interface to a zone; it needs an interface and does not set the default.
distractors.D: --get-default-zone READS the current default and takes no value; '=dmz' is invalid.

explanation.exam_pattern: Zones: '--get-active-zones' to view, '--set-default-zone=<z>' to change the catch-all default.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — firewalld zones (--set-default-zone)

questions.stem: On Ubuntu with ufw, you want to set the baseline policy to DENY all inbound traffic by default (then selectively allow services). Which command sets that default?

explanation.correct: ufw default deny incoming sets the catch-all inbound policy to deny; specific 'ufw allow' rules then permit the services you choose.

distractors.B: 'ufw disable' turns the firewall OFF entirely; 'disable incoming' is not valid.
distractors.C: 'ufw deny incoming' is not the default-policy syntax; the policy keyword is 'default'.
distractors.D: 'ufw reset' wipes all rules back to defaults; it does not set a deny policy for inbound.

explanation.exam_pattern: ufw baseline: 'ufw default deny incoming' + 'ufw default allow outgoing', then 'ufw allow <svc>'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — ufw default policy

questions.stem: Using the modern nftables tool, which command prints the ENTIRE active ruleset (all tables, chains, and rules) in one listing? (full command, three words)

explanation.correct: nft list ruleset dumps every table, chain, and rule currently loaded in the kernel's nftables engine — the nftables equivalent of 'iptables -S' for the whole system.
explanation.exam_pattern: nftables: 'nft list ruleset' (everything), 'nft list table <family> <name>' (one table); add rules with 'nft add rule'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — nftables (nft list ruleset)

questions.stem: After deploying SSH keys to all users, you want to FORCE key-based authentication by disabling password logins. Which sshd_config directive does this?

explanation.correct: PasswordAuthentication no makes sshd reject password logins, so only key-based (or other configured) authentication succeeds; restart sshd to apply.

distractors.B: PermitEmptyPasswords no only blocks accounts with BLANK passwords; normal passwords still work.
distractors.C: ChallengeResponseAuthentication governs keyboard-interactive/OTP methods, not ordinary password auth by itself.
distractors.D: UsePAM no disables the PAM stack (affecting account/session handling) and is not the switch for password login.

explanation.exam_pattern: Keys-only SSH: 'PasswordAuthentication no' (plus PermitRootLogin no); reload sshd after editing.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SSH hardening (PasswordAuthentication)

questions.stem: From your workstation you need to reach a database on the remote server's localhost:5432 by connecting to your own local port 5432, tunneled over SSH. Which command sets up that local port forward?

explanation.correct: ssh -L local_port:host:host_port forwards a LOCAL port through the SSH connection; '-L 5432:localhost:5432' makes your localhost:5432 reach the server's own localhost:5432.

distractors.B: -R is a REMOTE forward (opens a port on the server that tunnels back to you) — the opposite direction.
distractors.C: -D creates a SOCKS dynamic proxy, not a fixed port-to-host forward.
distractors.D: -X enables X11 forwarding for GUI apps, not a TCP port tunnel.

explanation.exam_pattern: SSH tunnels: -L local forward, -R remote forward, -D dynamic SOCKS proxy.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SSH tunneling (ssh -L)

questions.stem: Which sshd_config directive restricts SSH logins so that ONLY the users alice and bob may authenticate (everyone else is refused)?

explanation.correct: AllowUsers lists the only accounts permitted to log in via SSH; if present, any user not listed is denied.

distractors.A: PermitUsers is not a valid sshd_config directive.
distractors.B: AllowGroups restricts by GROUP membership, not by these specific usernames (alice/bob here are users, not groups).
distractors.D: DenyUsers would BLOCK alice and bob while allowing everyone else — the opposite of the requirement.

explanation.exam_pattern: sshd access lists: AllowUsers/AllowGroups (whitelist) vs DenyUsers/DenyGroups (blacklist); Allow wins when set.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SSH access control (AllowUsers)

questions.stem: You frequently run 'ssh web' and want it to connect as user deploy to host 10.0.0.9 on port 2222 using a specific key. In which file do you define this per-host CLIENT alias?

explanation.correct: The per-user client file ~/.ssh/config defines Host blocks with HostName, User, Port, and IdentityFile, so 'ssh web' expands to the full connection details.

distractors.B: ~/.ssh/known_hosts stores the host keys of servers you've connected to; it is not for aliases.
distractors.C: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys lists public keys permitted to log IN to this account; it is server-side, not a client alias.
distractors.D: /etc/ssh/sshd_config configures the SSH SERVER daemon, not the client's host aliases.

explanation.exam_pattern: Client shortcuts/options = ~/.ssh/config (Host/HostName/User/Port/IdentityFile); server options = sshd_config.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SSH client config (~/.ssh/config)

questions.stem: A user copied their public key to a server but key-based login still prompts for a password. The server's sshd has StrictModes on. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The ~/.ssh directory or authorized_keys file has overly open permissions (e.g., group/world-writable)
The private key was copied to the server instead of the public key

explanation.correct: With StrictModes on, sshd refuses to use keys if ~/.ssh (should be 700) or authorized_keys (should be 600) are too permissive, silently falling back to passwords.

distractors.B: authorized_keys must contain the PUBLIC key; while copying the private key is wrong, sshd would still read a valid public key — permissions are the classic StrictModes failure.
distractors.C: ssh_config is the client file; its absence does not block server-side key auth, and sshd uses sshd_config.
distractors.D: PermitRootLogin only affects the root account, not an ordinary user's key login.

explanation.exam_pattern: Key auth silently falls back to password => fix perms: chmod 700 ~/.ssh, chmod 600 authorized_keys (StrictModes).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — SSH key permissions (StrictModes)

questions.stem: You downloaded an ISO and the vendor published its SHA-256 checksum. Which command computes the ISO's hash so you can compare it against the published value for integrity?

explanation.correct: sha256sum distro.iso prints the file's SHA-256 digest; if it matches the vendor's published value the download is intact. ('sha256sum -c FILE.sha256' checks it automatically.)

distractors.B: openssl genrsa GENERATES an RSA private key; it does not hash a file.
distractors.C: md5sum -c expects a checksum FILE as input and MD5 is weak; the task calls for computing a SHA-256 hash.
distractors.D: gpg --encrypt protects CONFIDENTIALITY; it does not produce a verification checksum.

explanation.exam_pattern: Integrity check: sha256sum <file> and compare, or 'sha256sum -c <file>.sha256'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Integrity verification (sha256sum)

questions.stem: To troubleshoot a TLS handshake, you need to connect to the live service at www.example.com:443 and view the certificate chain it presents. Which OpenSSL command does this?

explanation.correct: openssl s_client -connect host:443 opens a TLS connection and prints the presented certificate chain and handshake details, ideal for diagnosing a live endpoint.

distractors.A: openssl verify checks a certificate FILE against a CA chain; it does not connect to a server.
distractors.B: openssl req works with certificate signing REQUESTS and has no -connect option.
distractors.C: openssl x509 parses a certificate FILE; it cannot take a host:port to connect to.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inspect a live TLS endpoint: 'openssl s_client -connect host:443'; inspect a cert file: 'openssl x509 -in file -text'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — TLS troubleshooting (openssl s_client)

questions.stem: A project ships release.tar.gz with a detached signature release.tar.gz.asc. After importing the maintainer's public key, which command verifies that the signature is valid for the file?

explanation.correct: gpg --verify <signature> <file> checks the detached signature against the file using the signer's imported public key, confirming authenticity and integrity.

distractors.A: sha256sum only hashes the signature file; it does not validate a GPG signature.
distractors.B: --sign CREATES a signature; it does not verify an existing one.
distractors.C: --decrypt is for encrypted content; a detached signature is not an encrypted payload.

explanation.exam_pattern: Verify a detached signature: 'gpg --verify file.asc file' (import the signer's public key first).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Signature verification (gpg --verify)

questions.stem: Which configuration file lists LUKS-encrypted block devices to be unlocked automatically early in boot (the encryption counterpart to /etc/fstab)? (full path)

explanation.correct: /etc/crypttab maps each encrypted device (name, backing device, key file, and options) so systemd unlocks it at boot; the resulting /dev/mapper device is then mounted via /etc/fstab.
explanation.exam_pattern: LUKS auto-unlock at boot = /etc/crypttab; the decrypted mapper device is mounted via /etc/fstab.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Disk encryption (/etc/crypttab)

questions.stem: A LUKS volume was unlocked as /dev/mapper/vault and has already been unmounted. Which command removes the decrypted mapping so the data is locked again?

explanation.correct: cryptsetup luksClose vault (equivalently 'cryptsetup close vault') tears down the /dev/mapper/vault mapping, so the plaintext device disappears and the volume is locked.

distractors.B: luksOpen UNLOCKS a device (creates the mapping) — the opposite of what is needed.
distractors.C: umount detaches a mounted filesystem but leaves the decrypted mapper device active.
distractors.D: luksFormat would REINITIALIZE the LUKS header, destroying the data.

explanation.exam_pattern: LUKS lifecycle: luksOpen (unlock) -> mount -> umount -> luksClose (lock/remove mapping).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 2 — Disk encryption (cryptsetup luksClose)

questions.stem: Inside a Bash script invoked as './deploy.sh prod', which variable expands to the first positional argument, 'prod'?

explanation.correct: $1 is the first positional parameter (here 'prod'); $2 would be the second, and so on.

distractors.A: $0 is the script's own name/path ('./deploy.sh'), not the first argument.
distractors.B: $# is the COUNT of arguments, not their values.
distractors.C: $* expands to ALL the positional parameters joined, not just the first.

explanation.exam_pattern: $0 script name, $1..$9 positional args, $# count, $@/$* all args, 'shift' drops $1.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Positional parameters ($1)

questions.stem: Which syntax captures the OUTPUT of the 'date +%F' command into the variable TODAY in a modern, nestable way?

explanation.correct: $(command) is command substitution: it runs the command and substitutes its stdout. It is preferred over backticks because it nests cleanly.

distractors.B: ${ ... } is parameter/variable expansion, not command execution.
distractors.C: ( ... ) without the leading $ creates an ARRAY from the words, not command output.
distractors.D: $[ ... ] is an obsolete ARITHMETIC form; it does not run commands (and is deprecated in favor of $(( )) ).

explanation.exam_pattern: Command substitution = $(cmd) (preferred) or `cmd` (legacy backticks); arithmetic = $(( expr )).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Command substitution ($( ))

questions.stem: You want a command's error messages (stderr) to be written to the SAME place its normal output (stdout) already goes — a log file. Which redirection achieves this?

explanation.correct: First '> app.log' points stdout (fd 1) at the file, then '2>&1' makes stderr (fd 2) follow fd 1 to the same file. Order matters: redirect stdout before duplicating it.

distractors.A: '>&1' here is evaluated before stdout is set to the file, so streams don't both land in app.log as intended.
distractors.C: 1>&2 sends stdout to wherever stderr points (the terminal), the reverse of the goal.
distractors.D: '2>1' redirects stderr to a FILE literally named '1', not to file descriptor 1 (that needs the &).

explanation.exam_pattern: Merge streams: 'cmd > file 2>&1' (stdout to file, then stderr to stdout). The & marks a descriptor.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Redirection (2>&1)

questions.stem: Which Bash construct correctly assigns the integer SUM of 5 and 3 to the variable TOTAL?

explanation.correct: $(( expression )) performs integer arithmetic and substitutes the result, so TOTAL becomes 8.

distractors.A: Bash would try to assign '5' and then run '+' and '3' as a command; it does not do math here.
distractors.B: $( ) is command substitution; it would try to EXECUTE '5' as a command and fail.
distractors.D: Quoting makes TOTAL the literal string '5 + 3', with no arithmetic performed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Integer math: $(( expr )); also 'let x=5+3' or (( x = 5 + 3 )). Floating point needs bc/awk.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Arithmetic expansion ($(( )))

questions.stem: Which test correctly checks, in an if statement, whether the regular file /etc/app.conf EXISTS before the script reads it?

explanation.correct: -f is true when the path exists AND is a regular file, the correct existence check before reading a config file.

distractors.A: -z tests whether a STRING is empty, not whether a file exists.
distractors.B: -x tests whether a file is EXECUTABLE; a config file need not be executable.
distractors.D: -d tests for a DIRECTORY; a config file is not a directory.

explanation.exam_pattern: File tests: -e exists, -f regular file, -d directory, -r readable, -s non-empty, -x executable.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — File test operators ([ -f ])

questions.stem: Which loop reads the file hosts.txt one line at a time, placing each line in the variable 'line' for processing, and handles lines without a trailing newline safely?

options.text: while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < hosts.txt
while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done | hosts.txt
read hosts.txt | while line; do echo "$line"; done
for line in hosts.txt; do echo "$line"; done

explanation.correct: 'while read -r line; do ...; done < file' reads each line into 'line' (the -r keeps backslashes literal) and the '< file' feeds the file on stdin, including a final unterminated line in most cases.

distractors.B: A pipe sends the loop's OUTPUT to hosts.txt as a command; it does not feed the file INTO the loop.
distractors.C: 'read hosts.txt' reads a line into a variable literally named hosts.txt; the syntax is wrong.
distractors.D: for iterates over the single word 'hosts.txt' (the filename), not its contents.

explanation.exam_pattern: Read a file line-by-line: 'while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file' (redirect in, not pipe).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Reading input (while read)

questions.stem: In the command 'mkdir /data && cd /data', what does the && operator guarantee?

options.text: Both commands always run regardless of outcome
cd /data runs only if mkdir /data succeeded (exit status 0)
cd /data runs only if mkdir /data failed
The two commands run simultaneously in parallel

explanation.correct: && is logical AND: the right-hand command executes only when the left-hand command exits 0 (success), so cd runs only if the directory was created.

distractors.A: ';' separates commands to always run both; && conditions the second on the first's success.
distractors.C: That describes ||  (logical OR), which runs the right side only when the left side FAILS.
distractors.D: && is sequential, not parallel; '&' (single) is what backgrounds a command.

explanation.exam_pattern: cmd1 && cmd2 (run cmd2 if cmd1 succeeds); cmd1 || cmd2 (run cmd2 if cmd1 fails); ';' = always.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Conditional execution (&&)

questions.stem: In a script, you want ${PORT} to use the value of the PORT variable if it is set, but fall back to 8080 when PORT is unset or empty — WITHOUT permanently assigning PORT. Which expansion does this?

explanation.correct: ${PORT:-8080} substitutes 8080 when PORT is unset or empty but leaves PORT itself unchanged — a read-only default.

distractors.B: := also ASSIGNS 8080 to PORT as a side effect, which the requirement forbids.
distractors.C: :? prints an error and exits if PORT is unset; it does not provide a usable default value.
distractors.D: :+ returns 8080 only when PORT IS set (the opposite condition), otherwise nothing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Defaults: ${v:-x} use x if unset; ${v:=x} use AND assign x; ${v:+x} x only if set; ${v:?msg} error if unset.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Parameter expansion (${var:-default})

questions.stem: Which redirection APPENDS a line to /var/log/app-custom.log without truncating the file, while discarding any error output?

explanation.correct: >> appends to the file (preserving existing contents), and '2>/dev/null' throws away stderr by sending it to the null device.

distractors.A: '<' redirects the file as INPUT to echo (which ignores stdin); it writes nothing to the log.
distractors.C: This appends, but '2>&1' sends errors INTO the log rather than discarding them.
distractors.D: A single '>' TRUNCATES the log to just this line, losing prior entries.

explanation.exam_pattern: >> append, > overwrite/truncate; 2>/dev/null discards errors; /dev/null = the bit bucket.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Redirection (append, /dev/null)

questions.stem: Which command creates a new branch named 'hotfix' AND immediately switches your working tree to it, in one step?

explanation.correct: git checkout -b hotfix (modern equivalent: 'git switch -c hotfix') creates the branch and checks it out together.

distractors.B: git switch hotfix (without -c) tries to switch to an EXISTING branch and errors if it doesn't exist.
distractors.C: git branch hotfix only CREATES the branch; you remain on the current one until you check out.
distractors.D: git merge integrates another branch's history; '-b' is not a merge option and it does not create branches.

explanation.exam_pattern: Create+switch: 'git checkout -b <name>' or 'git switch -c <name>'; 'git branch <name>' only creates.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Branching (git checkout -b)

questions.stem: What is the key difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?

options.text: git fetch uploads your commits; git pull downloads commits
git fetch downloads remote commits but does NOT merge them; git pull fetches AND merges into your branch
git fetch merges immediately; git pull only downloads

explanation.correct: git fetch updates your remote-tracking refs without changing your working branch; git pull is essentially 'fetch then merge' (or rebase), so it also integrates the changes.

distractors.A: Neither uploads; 'git push' uploads commits. Both fetch and pull download.
distractors.B: They differ: only pull modifies your current branch by merging.
distractors.D: Reversed: fetch does NOT merge; pull is the one that merges.

explanation.exam_pattern: fetch = download only (safe); pull = fetch + merge/rebase (updates your branch); push = upload.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Remotes (git fetch vs pull)

questions.stem: A bad commit was already pushed to the shared main branch. Which command creates a NEW commit that undoes that commit's changes, preserving history (safe for shared branches)?

explanation.correct: git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of the target commit, undoing it without rewriting history — the safe choice on a branch others have pulled.

distractors.A: git reset --hard rewrites history by moving the branch pointer; on a shared branch this forces others into conflicts.
distractors.B: git rm removes FILES from the tree/index; it does not undo a specific commit.
distractors.D: git checkout <commit> just moves you to that commit (detached HEAD); it does not undo anything.

explanation.exam_pattern: Undo a PUSHED commit safely = git revert (adds an inverse commit); git reset rewrites history (local only).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Undoing changes (git revert)

questions.stem: Which file, placed in a Git repository, lists path patterns (such as *.log or build/) that Git should leave UNTRACKED and not stage? (file name only)

explanation.correct: .gitignore contains glob patterns for files/directories Git should ignore, keeping build artifacts, logs, and secrets out of the repository.
explanation.exam_pattern: Exclude files from tracking with .gitignore (patterns, one per line; '!' re-includes; 'dir/' a folder).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Ignoring files (.gitignore)

questions.stem: You have uncommitted changes but must quickly switch branches to fix something else. Which command shelves your changes away (reverting the working tree to a clean HEAD) so you can reapply them later?

explanation.correct: git stash saves your modified tracked files onto a stash stack and restores a clean working tree; 'git stash pop' reapplies them afterward.

distractors.A: git clean -fd DELETES untracked files/directories; it does not preserve your changes.
distractors.C: git commit -a records the changes permanently instead of temporarily shelving them.
distractors.D: git reset --hard DISCARDS your changes entirely, with no way to reapply them.

explanation.exam_pattern: Temporarily shelve work = git stash; reapply with 'git stash pop' (or 'git stash apply').

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Stashing (git stash)

questions.stem: A container named 'web' is running and you need an interactive Bash shell inside it to investigate. Which command opens that shell?

explanation.correct: docker exec runs a new process in an ALREADY-running container; -i keeps stdin open and -t allocates a TTY, giving you an interactive shell. (podman exec is identical.)

distractors.B: docker attach connects to the container's main process stdio; it cannot launch a separate bash and can disrupt PID 1.
distractors.C: docker start restarts a stopped container and does not take a command to run interactively.
distractors.D: docker run creates a NEW container from an image; it does not attach to the existing 'web' container.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shell into a RUNNING container: 'docker exec -it <name> bash' (or sh); 'run' is for new containers.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Containers (docker exec -it)

questions.stem: A container 'api' exited immediately after starting. Which command shows the stdout/stderr it produced so you can see why it crashed?

explanation.correct: docker logs <container> prints the captured stdout/stderr of the container's main process, usually revealing the startup error; add -f to follow and --tail N to limit.

distractors.B: docker inspect dumps configuration/metadata JSON, not the application's console output.
distractors.C: docker ps lists containers; it does not show a container's log output.
distractors.D: docker events streams the daemon's lifecycle events, not an individual container's stdout.

explanation.exam_pattern: Diagnose a crashed container with 'docker logs <name>' (podman logs); -f follow, --tail to trim.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Containers (docker logs)

questions.stem: From a directory containing a Dockerfile, which command BUILDS an image and tags it myapp:1.0 using the current directory as the build context?

explanation.correct: docker build reads the Dockerfile in the context path ('.'), and -t myapp:1.0 names and tags the resulting image. (podman build uses the same options.)

distractors.A: docker create makes a container (without starting it) from an image; it does not build an image.
distractors.B: docker commit snapshots a running container into an image; it is not the Dockerfile build workflow.
distractors.C: docker run starts a CONTAINER from an existing image; it does not build one, and -t there allocates a TTY.

explanation.exam_pattern: Build+tag: 'docker build -t name:tag <context>'; the final '.' is the build context directory.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Containers (docker build -t)

questions.stem: In a Dockerfile, which instruction sets the DEFAULT command that runs when the container starts and can be easily OVERRIDDEN by arguments passed to 'docker run'?

explanation.correct: CMD provides the default command/arguments for a started container, and anything you append to 'docker run <image> ...' replaces it.

distractors.A: ENTRYPOINT sets a fixed executable that run-time arguments are APPENDED to (not replaced), so it is less easily overridden than CMD.
distractors.B: EXPOSE merely documents which ports the container listens on; it runs nothing.
distractors.D: RUN executes commands at BUILD time to create image layers; it is not the container's start command.

explanation.exam_pattern: CMD = default, overridable command; ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable (args appended); RUN = build-time step.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Dockerfile (CMD vs ENTRYPOINT)

questions.stem: You removed a stopped container but the disk is still full of images. Which command deletes the IMAGE named 'oldimage:latest' (not a container)?

explanation.correct: docker rmi (remove image) deletes an image; docker rm removes CONTAINERS. They are distinct object types, which the exam loves to test.

distractors.A: docker prune (e.g., 'docker image prune') removes UNUSED objects in bulk and does not take a specific image name like this.
distractors.B: docker rm removes a stopped CONTAINER, not an image.
distractors.D: docker stop halts a running container; it deletes nothing.

explanation.exam_pattern: rm = remove container; rmi = remove image; 'docker image prune' / 'system prune' bulk-cleans unused data.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Containers (docker rmi)

questions.stem: Which command runs the tasks defined in the Ansible playbook site.yml against the hosts listed in the inventory file 'hosts'?

explanation.correct: ansible-playbook runs a playbook; -i names the inventory. 'ansible-playbook -i hosts site.yml' executes site.yml's plays against the inventory hosts.

distractors.A: The bare 'ansible' command runs AD-HOC modules (e.g., 'ansible all -m ping'); it does not execute a playbook file.
distractors.B: ansible-galaxy installs roles/collections; 'run' is not how you execute a playbook.
distractors.D: ansible-vault encrypts/decrypts secret files; it does not run playbooks.

explanation.exam_pattern: Run a playbook: 'ansible-playbook -i <inventory> <playbook.yml>'; ad-hoc tasks use 'ansible <hosts> -m <module>'.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Ansible (ansible-playbook)

questions.stem: In an Ansible playbook, you want nginx to restart ONLY when a task actually changes its config file. Which mechanism links the config task to the restart action?

options.text: A loop over the service name
A handler that the config task triggers with 'notify'
A separate play that always runs 'service restart'
The 'when: always' conditional on the restart task

explanation.correct: Handlers run only when notified by a task that reports 'changed'. The config task uses 'notify: Restart nginx', and the handler runs once at the end of the play if a change occurred.

distractors.A: A loop repeats a task over items; it does not tie an action to a change event.
distractors.C: An always-restart play defeats idempotency, restarting even when nothing changed.
distractors.D: 'when: always' would run the restart every time, not only on change.

explanation.exam_pattern: Change-triggered actions in Ansible = notify + handlers; handlers fire once, at end of play, only if notified.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Ansible (handlers/notify)

questions.stem: What distinguishes an entry in the system-wide /etc/crontab (or a file in /etc/cron.d) from a line created with 'crontab -e' for a user?

options.text: The /etc/crontab line omits the minute field
The /etc/crontab line has an extra field naming the USER the job runs as, between the day-of-week and the command
The /etc/crontab line uses seconds instead of minutes

explanation.correct: System crontabs (/etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/*) add a user field after the five time fields, so the format is 'min hour dom mon dow USER command'. Per-user crontabs omit it (they already belong to a user).

distractors.A: @reboot is an optional special schedule available in both; it is not required in /etc/crontab.
distractors.B: Both formats keep all five time fields including the minute; none is omitted.
distractors.D: Standard cron has no seconds field in either location.

explanation.exam_pattern: System crontab = 6 fields incl. a USER column; 'crontab -e' user crontab = 5 time fields + command.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Scheduling (/etc/crontab user field)

questions.stem: A playbook needs to store a database password in version control safely. Which Ansible tool encrypts a variables file so its contents are not stored in plaintext?

explanation.correct: ansible-vault encrypt protects a file (e.g., secrets.yml) with a vault password; the ciphertext can be committed, and playbooks decrypt it at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or a vault file.

distractors.B: ansible-playbook has no --encrypt option; it RUNS playbooks (and can prompt for the vault password).
distractors.C: gpg has no --ansible mode; Ansible's own secret store is ansible-vault.
distractors.D: ansible-galaxy manages roles/collections, not secret encryption.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encrypt Ansible secrets with ansible-vault (encrypt/decrypt/view/edit); run with --ask-vault-pass or --vault-id.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 3 — Ansible (ansible-vault)

questions.stem: After a filesystem error, the root filesystem was mounted READ-ONLY and services can't write. You have fixed the underlying issue. Which command remounts / as read-write without rebooting?

explanation.correct: mount -o remount,rw / changes the mount options of the already-mounted root filesystem in place, switching it to read-write.

distractors.A: 'remount' is not a standalone command; remounting is 'mount -o remount,...'.
distractors.B: A plain mount of the device without 'remount' fails because / is already mounted (busy).
distractors.D: mount -a mounts fstab entries that aren't mounted; it won't flip an already-mounted root from ro to rw.

explanation.exam_pattern: Flip a mounted fs's options live: 'mount -o remount,rw <mountpoint>' (common recovery for a ro root).

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 4 — Storage troubleshooting (remount,rw)

questions.stem: A large log file was deleted to free space, but 'df' still shows the filesystem full. The space is not reclaimed because a process still holds the deleted file open. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Run 'sync' repeatedly until the space returns
Identify the holding process (e.g., lsof | grep deleted) and restart/stop it so the file handle closes
Delete the file again with rm -f

explanation.correct: Space is freed only when the LAST open handle to a deleted file closes. Find the holder with 'lsof | grep deleted' (or 'lsof +L1') and restart/stop it to release the space.

distractors.A: sync flushes buffers to disk; it does not release a file still held open by a process.
distractors.C: df -i only REPORTS inode usage; it does not delete inodes or free the held blocks.
distractors.D: The file is already gone from the directory; rm cannot act on it again and would not help.

explanation.exam_pattern: Deleted file but space not freed => a process holds it open. 'lsof | grep deleted', then restart that process.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 4 — Storage troubleshooting (open deleted files)

questions.stem: An XFS data filesystem on /dev/sdb1 is corrupt. It is unmounted. Which command checks and repairs an XFS filesystem (note that fsck.xfs does nothing on XFS)?

explanation.correct: XFS is repaired with xfs_repair on an UNMOUNTED device; fsck.xfs intentionally does nothing because XFS integrity is handled by log replay and xfs_repair.

distractors.B: e2fsck is the ext2/3/4 checker; wrong filesystem family for XFS.
distractors.C: mkfs.xfs REFORMATS the device, destroying all data rather than repairing it.
distractors.D: fsck.ext4 is for EXT filesystems; it cannot repair XFS.

explanation.exam_pattern: Repair by fs type: ext -> e2fsck/fsck.ext4; XFS -> xfs_repair (unmounted); fsck.xfs is a no-op.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 4 — Filesystem repair (xfs_repair)

questions.stem: A disk is throwing read errors and you suspect it is failing. Which command queries the drive's built-in SMART data to report its overall health?

explanation.correct: smartctl -H (from smartmontools) reports the drive's SMART overall-health self-assessment (PASSED/FAILED); 'smartctl -a' shows all attributes and error logs.

distractors.B: blkid shows UUID/filesystem type, not hardware health.
distractors.C: hdparm -T measures cached read SPEED; it does not read SMART health.
distractors.D: fdisk -l lists partition tables, not drive health.

explanation.exam_pattern: Disk health = SMART: 'smartctl -H' (summary) / 'smartctl -a' (full attributes), from smartmontools.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 4 — Disk health (smartctl)

questions.stem: Which sysstat-era tool gives a top-like, real-time view of disk I/O broken down BY PROCESS, so you can see which process is hammering the disk? (command name only)

explanation.correct: iotop shows per-process read/write throughput in real time (requires root), pinpointing the specific process responsible for heavy disk I/O.
explanation.exam_pattern: Per-process disk I/O = iotop; system/per-device I/O = iostat; high %iowait = storage bottleneck.

references: CompTIA Linux+ XK0-006 Objectives: Domain 4 — I/O troubleshooting (iotop)

questions.stem: A partition is full and you must locate the individual files larger than 500 MB under /var so you can archive or remove them. Which command lists them?

explanation.correct: find /var -type f -size +500M matches regular files larger than 500 MiB; the leading '+' means 'greater than'.

distractors.A: du has no -size filter; it totals directory sizes, not individual files by threshold.
distractors.B: '-size 500M' (no sign) matches files of EXACTLY 500M in the rounded unit, missing most large files.
